title: The embodied life of an early modern woman
gist: Reviewing Erin Maglaque's Presence: A Hidden History of the Female Body (Jonathan Cape, £25), Katherine Harvey argues the book convincingly traces today's most troubling attitudes to the female body — thinness as virtue, breastfeeding as norm, life beginning at conception — to specific 18th-century inflection points, while flagging that Maglaque sometimes overstates how novel that century was and that the archive itself is skewed by male voices and court records.

insights.claim: Erin Maglaque reoriented her scholarship after giving birth in her thirties, searching early modern archives for how women ate, slept, had sex and babies, washed, worked and died — treating the body rather than the mind as the historical subject.
insights.speaker: Katherine Harvey
insights.so_what: A reusable research move: personal experience as a lens that surfaces evidence categories a field has systematically ignored.
insights.locator: As a young scholar, the historian Erin Maglaque

insights.claim: The source material is frustratingly fragmentary, so Maglaque's method is to combine glimpses — a Cornish servant writing 'with the Child in my arms', Bridget Tomkyns fearing 'the loosing of her sences for lack of slepe' — with autobiographical interludes to construct a portrait.
insights.speaker: Katherine Harvey
insights.so_what: Where the archive is thin, composite anecdote plus authorial testimony becomes the operative evidentiary standard — with the reliability caveats that implies.
insights.locator: Though the material she uncovered was often frustratingly fragmentary

insights.claim: Reading early modern women's lives produces a constant oscillation between recognition and estrangement — familiar maternal experience sitting alongside beliefs that maternal imagination shaped a baby's features and that German courts ordered ugly individuals to stay home to avoid frightening pregnant women.
insights.speaker: Katherine Harvey
insights.so_what: A useful corrective against reading past societies as either wholly alien or reassuringly like us.
insights.locator: There is also much here that is strange

insights.claim: First-person accounts of female sexuality are extremely elusive because so much surviving evidence comes from court records, where women explaining relationships gone wrong were obliged to present themselves as weak and ignorant and male voices dominate.
insights.speaker: Katherine Harvey
insights.so_what: Evidence collected under adversarial legal incentives systematically distorts the behaviour it records — a bias worth naming in any archival dataset.
insights.locator: Such evocative turns of phrase greatly enliven the book

insights.claim: Because almost no early modern accounts of breastfeeding survive from a woman's perspective, the record is dominated by male writers who reveal their own moral preoccupations and sexual fantasies rather than the experience of nursing.
insights.speaker: Katherine Harvey
insights.so_what: What looks like historical evidence about women is often evidence about the men who wrote it down.
insights.quote: ‘the thrilling sensations… that accompany the act of giving suck.’
insights.locator: Similarly, since there are very few early modern accounts of breastfeeding

insights.claim: The assumption that maternal breastfeeding was the historical norm is false: in 1700 less than half of British mothers nursed their own children, with a lower figure in France, and even by 1800 the figure was still only around two thirds.
insights.speaker: Katherine Harvey
insights.so_what: Hard numbers overturning a supposed natural baseline — a reminder that 'traditional' practices are often recent inventions.
insights.locator: Though we now assume that maternal breastfeeding was the historical norm

insights.claim: The cult of sentimental motherhood had hardened by 1800 to the point that women who did not feed their own children were labelled 'more cruell than seamonsters'.
insights.speaker: Katherine Harvey
insights.so_what: Shows how fast a statistical minority behaviour became a moral obligation — a template for how norms get manufactured.
insights.locator: Even by 1800, when the cult of sentimental motherhood

insights.claim: Maglaque sometimes overstates the originality of the 18th century, since medieval mothers had also been accused of being too vain and selfish to nurse their own children.
insights.speaker: Katherine Harvey
insights.so_what: The reviewer's principal analytical objection: periodisation claims about 'when it all started' usually leak backwards.
insights.locator: Maglaque’s arguments about early modern mothering sometimes overstate

insights.claim: Midwifery was transformed as the traditional female midwife — equipped with a birthing stool and, in extremis, a hook inserted into the baby's skull — was gradually replaced by the man-midwife with his clanking bag of metal tools including newly invented forceps.
insights.speaker: Katherine Harvey
insights.so_what: A canonical case of a professionalising male-credentialed technology displacing an incumbent female craft — the pattern repeats across trades.
insights.locator: Midwifery was transformed during the early modern period

insights.claim: Forceps saved lives yet terrified many women, a tension Maglaque captures by describing her own forceps delivery as feeling like 'being penetrated by the Enlightenment'.
insights.speaker: Katherine Harvey
insights.so_what: Technological progress and experienced violence are not opposites — a framing worth carrying into debates about medical intervention.

insights.claim: The Catholic Church's claim that it always considered abortion a mortal sin is historically false: for centuries it took little notice of procedures performed before quickening, and only in the 18th century was conception widely accepted as the start of life.
insights.speaker: Katherine Harvey
insights.so_what: A directly contested historical claim in a live political debate, with a datable inflection point rather than an ancient continuity.

insights.claim: The doctrinal shift had concrete institutional consequences: shrines specialising in the temporary revival of stillborn babies sprang up across Northern Italy and parts of France, and Cangiamila's Embriologia Sacra (1745) demanded post-mortem caesareans on any pregnant woman who died regardless of family wishes — a practice that became law in Sicily.
insights.speaker: Katherine Harvey
insights.so_what: Shows how quickly a theological premise about when life begins converts into compulsory state medical practice over a woman's body.
insights.locator: New shrines specialising in the temporary revival

insights.claim: The aesthetic valuation of body fat reversed within a century: Venetian brides were fattened up with sweets at the end of the 17th century and fat was praised for hiding 'the gaping Interstices of the Muscles', yet by the 1760s physicians were telling plumper patients to eat soap on the reasoning that it cleaned fat from the blood as it removed oil stains from linen.
insights.speaker: Katherine Harvey
insights.so_what: Beauty standards are demonstrably reversible within a lifetime — evidence against treating current aesthetic norms as biologically grounded.
insights.locator: At the end of the 17th century, Venetian brides

insights.claim: By the end of the 18th century a fashionable young woman's 'puny appetite' was read as proof of 'exquisite sensibility', founding the idea that a thin woman is a better woman which has shaped countless lives since — including Maglaque's grandmother, a talented home cook who starved herself for most of her life.
insights.speaker: Katherine Harvey
insights.so_what: The book's central and best-supported claim: modern body pathology has a datable origin in 18th-century medicine and fashion rather than being timeless.
insights.locator: By the end of the century, as fat became an aesthetic issue

themes.theme: Religion, night and the good death

insights.claim: Religious belief touched every bodily experience, so that reproductive lives were read through faith — Lady Sarah Cowper consoled herself she had conceived four children without an unchaste thought or sexual pleasure, while Alice Thornton saw childbirth as a martyrdom bringing her closer to God.
insights.speaker: Katherine Harvey
insights.so_what: Religious framing was the operating system through which physical suffering was interpreted, not an overlay on it.
insights.locator: Above all, religious belief touched and shaped every bodily experience

insights.claim: The early modern night was materially darker and more frightening than ours — street lighting and nightlife only appeared in the late 1700s, bad dreams were attributed to witches' curses, and insomnia was treated with highly effective but easily fatal opium-laced syrups.
insights.speaker: Katherine Harvey
insights.so_what: Infrastructure — here, artificial light — reshapes the psychological texture of daily life, a mechanism worth remembering when assessing any ambient technology.
insights.locator: Though both urban street lighting and (not unrelatedly) nightlife
